items.basis: Friction sliding introduces wear particles that will inevitably accumulate between interfaces, creating a third-body wear mechanism that accelerates degradation rather than preventing it, directly contradicting the claimed effect of reduced permanent deformation.

The sliding displacement limit of <300% of elastomer thickness is grossly inadequate for seismic events where bearings may experience displacements exceeding 1000% of thickness, violating the boundary condition of moderate seismic events.

The evidence [doi:10.1016/j.matpr.2020.12.328] shows that fatigue life in laminated bearings is primarily controlled by elastomer hysteresis and heat buildup, not interface sliding, directly contradicting the proposed mechanism as the primary failure mode.

The predicted <50% permanent deformation after 75-year equivalent testing is unsupported by any evidence in the bundle, as the baseline already incorporates friction dissipation through natural rubber-steel interfaces, making the claimed improvement unsubstantiated.

Creating a controlled sliding interface coefficient between elastomer layers and steel plates is impossible to maintain consistently across manufacturing tolerances, as evidenced by [doi:10.4028/www.scientific.net/amm.204-208.2244] which shows horizontal rigidity variations of ±15% in standard bearings.

The testable prediction fails to define what constitutes "optimized sliding interfaces" or specify the measurement protocol for wear particle accumulation, making the prediction untestable and unverifiable.
